newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Chip upstart says Intel can lead, not monopolise.
newsitem.headline: Chip upstart says Intel can lead, not monopolise.

text.p: One of several challengers to launch clones of Intel Corp's flagship Pentium chips conceded on Wednesday that the U.S. giant was all but unstoppable, but said the market opposed an Intel monopoly.

"Like it or not, Intel is a runaway freight train that no one can stop," said vice president Joe Baranowski of Centaur Technology, which designed the Pentium-class IDT-C6 chip launched in May by Integrated Device Technology.
"There is absolutely no way anyone can compete against Intel on the high-end, market-leading level," Baranowski told Reuters in an interview.
Baranowski, attending Computex '97, a premier trade show in Taipei, said manufacturers in Taiwan and elsewhere supported Intel -- but also were keen to hedge their bets.
"Computer and motherboard makers want alternatives to Intel, because they don't want their future to be determined by one company," he said.

Integrated Device and other Pentium clone-makers like Cyrix Corp were hoping to use the five-day Taipei expo to persuade Taiwan's world-leading motherboard makers to think twice about using Intel chips and try theirs instead.
A sampling of Taiwan motherboard makers said they were going both ways, designing boards to accommodate standard Socket 7 processors as well as Intel's new vertical-insert design.

Intel, whose Pentium chips corner over 80 percent of the world microchip market, on Monday unveiled the first of its second-generation P-II Pentium series, which boasts a clock speed of 233 megahertz.

Integrated Device said its new IDT-C6 chip features Intel's multimedia-enhancing MMX technology and runs at a blistering 200 megahertz -- but, at US$100 in bulk, sells for a fraction of Pentium's US$594 bulk price.
"Intel is going to make chips faster and faster, but that does not mean it should dominate every single segment of the market," Baranowski said.
Integrated Device said it would make public at the end of June the names of Taiwan computer and motherboard partners who will be powering their products with the IDT-C6 chip.
"We cannot say anything specific right now, but what I can tell you is that there is a consensus call for a low-end alternative to Intel," Baranowski said.
Intel's new Pentium chip will appear in the third quarter in personal computers priced at $2,000 to $2,500. Integrated Device said its chip targets computers that sell around $1,000.
Other companies hoping to challenge Intel with Pentium clones at lower prices include International Business Machine, Advanced Micro Devices, International Meta Systems and National Semiconductor.
Integrated Device, however, remained sceptical about attempts to battle Intel at the lucrative high-end level.

"The only way you can survive alongside Intel is to not compete directly against its most advanced chip," Baranowski said. "The other companies are all trying to compete at over the 200-megahertz level. That will not work."
Even a tiny slice of the microchip pie would mean several hundred million dollars to a company like Integrated Device. With its four-fifths slice, Intel had revenues of $20.8 billion in 1996.
